articles.title: CMC observes World Stroke Day
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Interactive stalls, talks in four languages, testimonies from stroke survivors, and a reel-making competition were also held
The Christian Medical College (CMC) observed World Stroke Day 2026 at its campus in Vellore and Ranipet on Friday.

According to a press release, the event was held under the theme ‘Each Minute Counts, Be FAST, Recognise Stroke, Save Lives’. The celebrations brought together neurology, radiology, rehabilitation, emergency medicine, and nursing teams to show the public what timely stroke care looks like, from the first symptom to recovery.

A free Carotid Doppler screening camp run by the Division of Clinical Radiology, catered to around 500 persons. Interactive stalls, talks in four languages, testimonies from stroke survivors, and a reel-making competition were also held.

The event discussed warning signs of stroke, the urgency of reaching hospital within the treatment window, emergency brain imaging, acute treatment, including clot-dissolving and clot-retrieval therapies, and rehabilitation and recovery.

Vinay Timothy Oommen, deputy director, CMC Vellore, and head, Department of Physiology; Myla Yacob, deputy medical superintendent, CMC Vellore, are among others who took part in the event, the release said.

articles.title: BRS govt. fought Miyapur land case in SC, protected it: Harish Rao
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Says Congress Govt. is planning to sell the land now and terms it a disgrace

Deputy Floor Leader of the BRS Legislature Party and former minister T. Harish Rao has stated that the previous BRS Government had protected the 550 acres of government land in Miyapur, while the present Congress Government is planning to monetise it.

He mentioned that the BRS Government had fought the land case in the Supreme Court and saved it. However, Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy was planning to sell it now. After the Supreme Court verdict on the land in Miyapur, the Chief Minister held a press conference and everything he said there was contradictory to what was mentioned in the Supreme Court’s records.

The Miyapur dispute reached the Supreme Court as a Special Leave Petition (SLP) in 2003 and became a Civil Appeal in 2013, when the Congress was in power, but the party did nothing. After Telangana was formed, then Chief Minister K. Chandrasekhar Rao had ensured that the land in the heart of Hyderabad did not slip out of the government’s hands. In 2015, he engaged Senior Counsel C.S. Vaidyanathan to fight for the land in the government’s favour, he said.

Mr. Vaidyanathan appeared for Telangana from April 7, 2015 and argued for the protection of the Miyapur land. From 2015 to 2023, for nearly eight years, the BRS Government fought the case without a break. Every petition, every affidavit and every piece of evidence placed before the Supreme Court on Miyapur land was during the BRS tenure.

In its judgment on the land, the Supreme Court said: “It is apposite to discuss the relevant expressions and regulations under the A.P. Abolition of Jagirs Regulations and the Atiyat Inquiries Act. Certain relevant terminologies are being extracted from paragraph 93 of the judgment of this Court in Trinity Infraventures Ltd. v. M.S. Murthy, 2023 SCC OnLine SC 738, for the said purpose”.

So, the real foundation of the Miyapur land verdict was the Trinity Infraventures judgment. That case involving Goldstone Prasad was won by the Government of Telangana on June 15, 2023. “The victory that day and the legal grounds laid down in that judgment are what the Miyapur land verdict stands today,” Mr. Harish Rao said.

However, the Chief Minister held a press conference claiming it as his government’s victory and repeated falsehoods. The plan behind the victory claims and celebration was to sell the 550 acres land having the market value of about ₹60,000 crore now.

articles.title: Kashmir issue cannot be addressed through security approach alone, requires political engagement: Mirwaiz
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq said peace cannot simply be measured by the absence of protests

Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, in his Friday sermon at the historic Jama Masjid, said the Kashmir issue cannot be addressed through a security approach alone and requires “political engagement and efforts at reconciliation”.

“Our consistent position has been that the Kashmir issue cannot be addressed through a security approach alone. Political issues require political engagement, and longstanding grievances require sincere efforts at reconciliation,” said the Mirwaiz, in his Friday (October 30, 2026) address.

Referring indirectly to the Centre’s policy in Kashmir, the Mirwaiz said, “If the situation has improved, as is being acknowledged, should it not also be an opportunity to ease restrictions, review detentions, restore civil liberties and create an environment in which people can express their views and grievances peacefully?”

He said peace cannot simply be measured by the absence of protests. “If meaningful progress has been made in improving security, the next step should be to build upon it through reconciliation, release and review of political prisoners, restoration of civil liberties and sincere political engagement,” he added.

Referring to the recent report published by the International Crisis Group, an international advocacy group, the Mirwaiz said, “The findings of the report deserve serious attention. It calls for the restoration of Statehood, meaningful powers for the elected government, a review of stringent anti-terror laws and renewed dialogue between India and Pakistan.”
The Mirwaiz said that addressing security concerns alone cannot brush aside “aspirations of the people, who are equally important and must find a place in any meaningful process towards peace.”

Referring to the 2025 war between India and Pakistan, the Mirwaiz said, “The events of last year once again demonstrated the dangers of confrontation between India and Pakistan. We have always maintained that dialogue, rather than confrontation, remains the most responsible way forward. I raise these issues not in a spirit of confrontation, but out of genuine concern for the future of our people.”

He underlined that the “real measure of peace is not merely how much violence has declined, but how much trust has been restored”. “That is the message we should take from this report too,” said the Mirwaiz

The cleric, who once headed the separatist Hurriyat, said, “The report says that militancy, street protests and violence have declined in recent years, which everyone welcomes, as no one understands the value of peace more than the people of Kashmir, who have suffered enormously over the past several decades”.

He, however, added that Kashmir remains one of the most militarised places on earth. “One of the most disturbing aspects highlighted in the report is the scale of arrests and detentions since 2019. According to the Union Home Ministry’s own figures, 3,662 people were arrested under UAPA in J&K between 2019 and 2023, while only 23 convictions were recorded during that period. These figures raise serious questions about prolonged detention, due process and the widespread use of stringent laws,” said the Mirwaiz.
He said thousands of families suffer the consequences of arrests, detentions and prolonged legal proceedings. “They continue to live with uncertainty about the future of their loved ones,” he added.

He also expressed concern over the continued incarceration of Kashmiri political prisoners, including Yasin Malik, Shabir Ahmad Shah, Shahid Ul Islam , Engineer Rashid , Asiya Andrabi, Masrat Alam, and many others.

He said thousands of families suffer the consequences of arrests, detentions and prolonged legal proceedings. “They continue to live with uncertainty about the future of their loved ones,” he added.

He also expressed concern over the continued incarceration of Kashmiri political prisoners, including Yasin Malik, Shabir Ahmad Shah, Shahid Ul Islam , Engineer Rashid , Asiya Andrabi, Masrat Alam, and many others.

Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant’s exasperation, during the Supreme Court’s hearing on October 29 on the “digital arrest” scams, that people still fall for such scams despite abundant warnings and orders from the Court is understandable. About ₹800 crore has been lost to these scams this year even after recoveries, a hefty sum from the savings of individual victims. But this is not merely about gullibility. Scammers posing as CBI or police officers succeed because their victims, older citizens in particular, defer to or fear law enforcement. When Indian police are widely seen as high-handed towards ordinary citizens and as serving only the powerful, the threat of an “arrest” over a video call cannot be that implausible for many. That said, the Court’s pressing of the Reserve Bank of India to finalise its KYC Amendment Directions, 2026, which require banks to flag suspected mule accounts and put temporary debit holds on them, is welcome. CBI investigations have shown that mule accounts are central to scammers laundering their proceeds after duping victims and that bank staff have, in some cases, helped open them. With the availability of complete transaction histories and AI tools, banks can now spot anomalous transactions faster. The Attorney-General’s assurance that the directions will be in force by December 31 is also welcome. The Court’s insistence that banks compensate victims addresses an issue with the RBI’s zero-liability provisions. Its 2017 circular covers only unauthorised transactions, leaving victims who were coerced into making transfers without any recourse.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Constitutional & Policy Analysis: A critical evaluation of recent executive and judicial developments highlights the need for transparent implementation, federal cooperation, and statutory accountability across central and state institutions.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Digital News Publishers Association’s (DNPA) challenge to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 , and its Rules , has drawn attention to concerns that a law to safeguard informational privacy risks creating a serious chilling effect on the media. The absence of a specific exemption for journalistic activity could subject reporters investigating official misconduct or corruption to the obligations of a “data fiduciary”, requiring them to notify and seek consent from the very individuals they are investigating. Such onerous requirements could affect investigations undertaken in the public interest. The implications extend to routine newsgathering too, where personal information is integral to reporting. The omission is particularly consequential because the drafts in 2018, 2019 and 2021 carried a journalistic exemption. The Act already provides exemptions for certain forms of data processing, including for research and statistical purposes, making the denial of similar protection to journalists difficult to justify. Non-compliance can attract penalties of up to ₹250 crore, posing an existential threat to smaller and independent newsrooms. The DNPA petition also challenges Section 44(3), which amended the RTI Act, 2005, removing the earlier public-interest qualification concerning disclosure of personal information. The protection of personal information must not be absolute; an overriding public interest must remain a legitimate ground for disclosure, particularly when the information is held by public authorities. Investigations into corruption often rely on asset disclosures and tender documents containing personal data. Restricting access to these records risks reducing journalism to merely reproducing government releases.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: At Wednesday’s hearing of a petition on the Delhi SIR in the Supreme Court, Justice Joymalya Bagchi asked questions that cut to the heart of the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s SIR of electoral rolls . If an existing voter was “lax, inert or did not respond” to enumeration forms, was that a ground for the ECI to “forfeit his or her right to vote forever”? The Bench headed by the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said that the ECI was in “error” to force such voters, struck off for not returning enumeration forms, to reapply on Form 6 as if they were new voters. It asked why voters who had shifted residences could not just disclose details and why deleted voters could not fill enumeration forms belatedly. This is the central design flaw of the SIR as it shifts the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector, including those who have voted before, and treats a mere change of address as ground for deletion. The share of draft deletions recorded as “shifted” or “absent” rose from 55% in Bihar to 72% in States/Union Territories in Phase 3. In Karnataka, about 84 lakh electors were deleted, marked as “shifted” or “absent” during enumeration. But only a net of 8.2 lakh, including new electors, were added during the claims phase, with the final roll being 64.5 lakh short of the projected adult population. Requiring moved voters to re-register as fresh applicants defeats the ECI’s historic mandate of widening the franchise, which was inherent in the 2002-03 intensive revision, where enumerators enrolled shifted voters at their new homes and the Chief Electoral Officer reconciled the old entries.

This particular rapidity is a challenge for forecasters and some models did fail to anticipate how strong Arnab would become. It also moved faster than expected towards the coast, before stalling for a time and beginning the landfall process several hours before the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted it would, in the middle of the night, leaving many district authorities with a potentially narrower window to evacuate high-risk settlements. Chandrababu Naidu, said there were five deaths in Andhra Pradesh . Regrettably, the suspension of transport services, including road connectivity and flights, closure of schools and offices, and power cuts to minimise risks posed by loose wires remains an essential part of saving lives, entailing other social and economic disruptions that the States must account for, and address, in their post-storm assessments.
